EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
Many items we use everyday are controlled by microprocessors.
INTRODUCTIONM
Microprocessors have quietly found a place in our lives. We use them in modern transportation, microwave ovens, entertainment systems and calculators.
Another example of how microprocessors are used is light control. Microprocessors vary the window tint according to the light intensity.

Microprocessors are designed to accurately process information, perform repetitive actions and do so precisely the same way every time. They are extremely reliable and relatively inexpensive. In this lesson, we will examine a 32-bit 68000 microprocessor......
Let's begin the lesson on INTRODUCTION TO 68000 MICROPROCESSORS.............
LESSON MENU
There are three primary components to any microprocessor system; Central Processing Unit (CPU), Memory, Input and Output (I/O). Any of the three, alone, have no functional value.
DISCUSSION
Memory is a place where the CPU can store and recall information.
Input and output devices allow the CPU to communicate with a user or another device. This is how the CPU gets instructions and information to act on.

The CPU is the microprocessor of any system. It is responsible for performing instructions, controlling the system and maintaining operations. To achieve these requirements, the CPU employs a Control Unit, Registers and an Arithmetic Logic Unit.
REGISTERS
The Control Unit is the section of the CPU that directs all information passed to or from the CPU.
REGISTERS
Without accurate timing, information being processed by the CPU would get scrambled and blocked much like a Los Angeles traffic jam.

Because the CPU must handle enormous amounts of information simultaneously, it must have a place to temporarily store data while other information is being processed. The number of registers will vary from one CPU to the next. In the 68000, there are 20; 8 for data, 7 for addresses and 5 system registers.
REGISTERS

Digital electronics has been called the electronics of counting. Every function performed by a CPU, in some manner, involves the manipulation of binary numbers. Any mathematical operations in the CPU are performed by the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU).
REGISTERS

Now that we have examined the make-up of the CPU, our next focus will be memory. The memory section of a microprocessor system provides a large storage area for information. The information includes both programs and the data needed by the system to run the programs.
There are two types of memory used by the CPU; Read Only Memory and Random Access Memory. These are commonly known as ROM and RAM.

READ ONLY MEMORY - ROM is a nonvolatile form of memory. ROM can be accessed randomly. The program counter points to the location of the next instruction. The address of ROM can be changed randomly by changing the program counter.
DEFINITION

RANDOM ACCESS MEMORY - RAM is a form of memory. When power is off, all the data in RAM is destroyed. RAM is useful to store temporary data or important values generated by the computer. RAM also stores frequently used parts of contained in slower mass memory. RAM can be accessed randomly.
DEFINITION
The amount of memory used by a system varies greatly with need. Early home PC's typically had 640 kB of RAM. Today, this has increased to many millions of bytes.
As programs become larger and more elaborate, the amount of memory needed for smooth operation also grows. Because memory is expensive, most systems have only enough for their applications.

Memory is organized in a grid format known as a matrix. Every location in the matrix is assigned a unique address. In this way, the CPU is able to write or read from any particular location within memory.

The last section of a microprocessor system is I/O. The input/output section interfaces the CPU to the real world. I/O devices allow the user or the devices, themselves, to communicate with the CPU. The chart below lists many common I/O devices.
ROTATE LEFT
For the three sections of a microprocessor system to work properly, they need a conduit or some form of highway to pass information back and forth. This is accomplished through the use of buses.
A bus, in a microprocessor system, is a series of wires grouped by function and connected to various portions of the system; Address Bus, Data Bus and Control Bus.
24 - BIT ADDRESS BUS
16 - BIT DATA BUS

The address bus is used to carry the addresses generated by the CPU. As mentioned, the addresses indicate a location in memory or an I/O port. Address values for the 68000 microprocessor are 24 bits in length. This means they can have a value anywhere from 1 (2 ) to 16,777,216 (2 ), nearly 17 million locations!
Address buses are unidirectional. This means that the system's devices can only read from the address bus, not write to it.

The data bus is used to transfer information between different sections of the microprocessor system. Once the proper address has been selected by the CPU, data may be passed to or from the CPU via the data bus.

The data bus in the 68000 microprocessor is 16 bits long. This means that 16 bits of data may be transferred at one time. Unlike the address bus, the data bus is bi-directional. Data may be written to or read from the data bus.

The last bus that will be examined is the control bus. The control bus carries the signals that both synchronize and enable or disable certain functions of devices wishing to communicate with the CPU.
Some control signals are generated by the CPU while others are from the devices tied to it. As with the data bus, the control bus is bi-directional.
Now that you have been introduced to the major components of a microprocessor system, let's see how they work together.
A program is stored in memory, but the microprocessor needs a way to access the program. One of the system registers in the CPU, known as the program counter (PC), is used for this purpose.
ROTATE LEFT

The program counter holds the address of the next instruction for the program and directs the control section of the CPU to the location (address) of that instruction. The control section takes the address stored in the program counter and places it on the address bus.

The control section then signals to memory (through the control bus) that it's requesting the instruction at that memory location. The control section of the CPU then stores the instruction in the instruction register (IR).

After the instruction is stored in the instruction register, the control section must then decode it so that the CPU knows what it is being told to do. Once that is accomplished the CPU then performs the instruction and sets (increments) the program counter to the location of next instruction.

This process is repeated as each instruction of the program is requested. The time required to perform each instruction is based upon the system's clock speed and the number of cycles of the instruction. Buses and registers are of finite capacity, so some instructions require several cycles to complete them.
Microprocessors are often categorized by their clock speed and data size. For example, an eight bit data bus would be equal to an eight bit CPU, and so on. However, the 68000 CPU is an exception.

The 68000 has the ability to manage 8, 16, and 32 bits of data. The data bus however, only holds 16 bits, so if 32 bits of information are being sent the CPU must read the line twice to get all 32 bits from memory.

The names associated with the 8, 16, and 32 bit data groups are: byte for 8 bits, word for 16 bits and longword for 32 bits. All instructions used by the 68000 are words since it is limited to a 16 line data bus.

Microprocessors only understand binary, but binary numbers tend to be large and hard to enter accurately. The Hexadecimal or OP Code is much easier for an operator to enter CPU instructions. The CPU sends the OP Code to the instruction decoder where the hexadecimal is converted to binary.
Function OP Code Assembly Language Machine Language

Assembly language uses mnemonics (shortened versions of words that describe the action indicated by the instruction). In this way, the programmer is able to read through the program without having to memorize all of the OP Codes.
When in the Supervisor Mode, programs have control of the CPU and all system functions, this includes the operating system, interrupts and routines which manage I/O.

NUMBERING SYSTEMSLE

All microprocessors evaluate data in binary form. This means that they only recognize two voltage conditions: 1 and 0, 1 representing high voltage (typically 5 V) and 0 representing low voltage (typically 0 V).
DISCUSSION
Binary numbers are often large and hard to work with, so hexadecimal is commonly used in programming.
Converting from one number system to another is an essential skill needed by technicians and programmers.
A quick review of the decimal number system may refresh your understanding of other number systems.
Any quantity can be represented by using these ten symbols.

Other number systems use different sets of symbols. For example, binary has two symbols, 1 and 0, while hexadecimal uses sixteen, 0 through 9 plus A through F. Yet, the common factor between the systems is that any quantity may be represented regardless of the system used.

There are two methods used to distinguish between number systems. One method is to write the base (also known as the radix) as a subscript at the end of a number, such as 11001 or EAC24 . The other method is to designate the base by letter after the number as in FF64h or 1100011b.
2ourteennnnnnnennnnnnnnnnnnred sixty-fiveee
16urteennnnnnnennnnnnnnnnnnred sixty-fiveee

Throughout much of the world, the decimal system is the standard, so the radix of a decimal number is rarely indicated. Still, when working with different number systems, the base should always be shown to avoid confusion. Without the base, 10101 could be interpreted as binary, decimal or hexadecimal.

All modern number systems are positional, where each number's position indicates its relative value. In the decimal system, for example, each position has a value ten times greater than the one to its immediate right. This method of number representation is known as positional notation.
An example of a non-positional number system is the roman numeral system. In this system the value of a position varies as the count increases or decreases.

The left-most digit of any numerical quantity has the largest value in any positional number system. This digit is referred to as MSD (most significant digit) except for binary where it is called the most significant bit (MSB). The right-most digit is called the least significant digit (LSD) or LSB for binary.

Consider the decimal number 4356. The 4, the left-most digit, has a value of 4000, the 3, 300, the 5, 50 and 6 represents 6. The left-most digit has the greatest value while the 6 has the least. This number could be written as 4000 + 300 + 50 + 6 or in scientific notation as: (4x10 ) + (3x10 ) + (5x10 ) + (6x10 ).

We can illustrate this positional process by examining four baskets to represent decimal number position. The first basket, the right-most (LSD), represents the ones position; the second the tens position, the third the hundreds and the fourth (MSD) the thousands.

Reaching our break point requires all apples be removed from basket three and one apple be placed in basket four. The break- point is the same for all baskets. This procedure is identical for any positional number system, only the break-points and position values change. Let's try it with hexadecimal.

Once our position values have been assigned to the baskets, we can add apples. If we place 12 apples in the third basket and 2 in the first, we end up with C02 as our base 16 value. Remember, hexadecimal uses 0 - 9 and A - F. This makes the 12 apples in the third basket equal to C.

The binary to hex conversion breaks down the binary number into groups of four bits, often referred to as a nibble. A nibble has 16 possible combinations of 1's and 0's (0000 to 1111). Any one of the combinations can be represented by one hex number.

Conversion of hexadecimal numbers to decimal numbers can be accomplished using the same process you performed for binary to decimal conversion. However, progressing up through the powers of two is a lot easier than sixteen. It is simpler to first convert to binary and then to hexadecimal.

Even though microprocessors understand only binary data, we use this data to represent more than just numbers. Binary may be used to represent text, also. This is accomplished through the use of a pre-established code. One of the most widely used is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange).

To use ASCII chart, locate the letter or symbol that you need; the corresponding ASCII code for that character is located to the immediate left. Some ASCII charts provide the binary equivalent along with the hex. If it's not available, just convert the hex to binary as you did before.

Another commonly used code is known as BCD (Binary Coded Decimal). Unlike the ASCII code, BCD is used only to represent decimal numbers. BCD, in a sense, works similar to hexadecimal in that each BCD representation is a group of four binary bits.

Each four-bit group represents some decimal number between zero and nine. That is, no number greater than 9 can be represented by any singular BCD group. It is important to note that binary data in BCD format cannot be converted to decimal using the method learned earlier.

In BCD, each group of four bits is independent of the others in the number. This makes translating the binary to decimal easier for us, but complicates mathematical computations. Below is an example of BCD encoding.
